subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage:
“Wasim, come say hello to Uncle and Aunty.”
Wasim stood in the doorway of the new neighbours' flat with his arms pressed flat against his sides, hands tucked into his shorts pockets.
“Hello, Wasim!” said the aunty. “Want some juice?”
Wasim looked at Saurabh Chacha's knees and said nothing.
“He takes a little time,” Saurabh said. He crouched. “You can stay next to me. No rush.”
Wasim leaned on his leg. Twenty minutes later one hand came out of a pocket, and he pointed at the juice.

qa.q: Where did Wasim put his hands?
qa.a: He tucked them into his shorts pockets, with his arms pressed flat against his sides.

qa.q: What do Wasim's arms pressed to his sides suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he felt shy and cautious with new people in a new place. He might also have felt a bit overwhelmed by being greeted so directly.

qa.q: Which choice by Saurabh worked, and why?
qa.a: He let Wasim stay close and said there was no rush, so Wasim could warm up in his own time.

qa.q: How might the new aunty see Wasim's silence?
qa.a: She might wonder if he disliked her, but Saurabh's words help her see he just needs time.

grounding: A shy child keeps his arms tucked to his body around new people, and a familiar adult nearby helps him warm up.

subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage:
Settling-in note, day one. Written by Bhavna, nursery teacher.
Vidya arrived holding her father's finger. After he left, she stood by the cubbies with her arms folded tight against her chest and her elbows tucked in. When children came near, she pulled her arms in even closer. I didn't make her join. I sat on a low stool close to her and sorted crayons, humming. By snack time she had moved to my side. At going-home time she reached out, took a red crayon, and drew one circle.

qa.q: What colour crayon did Vidya take?
qa.a: A red crayon.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she pulled her arms in closer when children came near?
qa.a: She was probably shy and cautious, protecting herself in a new place without her father. She may also have been sad that he had left.

qa.q: What might Bhavna try on day two?
qa.a: Bhavna could sit near Vidya again and offer the crayons early, letting her join at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Vidya's father feel reading this note?
qa.a: He would likely feel reassured that the teacher was patient and that Vidya slowly began to relax.

grounding: The note shows a shy child keeping her arms tucked in around new people, and time and a nearby adult helping.

subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage: The naming ceremony filled the courtyard with relatives Payal had never met. She stood pressed against Bhavna Maasi, arms tight to her body, hands clasped at her tummy. When a loud uncle bent to pinch her cheek, she tucked her chin and pulled her elbows in. Maasi gently stepped between them. “She's still getting used to everyone.” She let Payal hold the end of her dupatta. By the time the sweets came round, Payal was holding out one hand for a laddoo.

qa.q: What did Bhavna Maasi let Payal hold?
qa.a: The end of her dupatta.

qa.q: Why did Payal pull her elbows in when the uncle bent down?
qa.a: She felt shy and uneasy with a loud stranger reaching for her face, and wanted to keep herself small and safe.

qa.q: What went right in how Maasi handled the uncle?
qa.a: She calmly stepped between them and explained, which protected Payal without making a scene.

qa.q: How might the loud uncle see Payal's pulled-in arms?
qa.a: He might think she is unfriendly, but Maasi's words help him understand she just needs time.

grounding: A shy child keeps her arms close to her body among new relatives, and a familiar aunt nearby helps.

passage: On the rooftop in Ahmedabad, Harsha's green kite was cut by a neighbour's string and drifted away over the tanks. Harsha's hands curled into tight fists. She stamped, face red. Vikas, her father, put down the spool. “You're angry. That was your best kite.” “I want to hit him!” “Hitting's not okay. But you can squeeze.” He handed her the soft rubber ball from his pocket. Harsha squeezed it hard, again and again. Slowly her fingers loosened, and she asked, “Can we fly the yellow one?”

qa.q: What colour was Harsha's kite that was cut?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What do Harsha's tight fists suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest she was angry and frustrated about losing her best kite. She may also have felt sad under the anger.

qa.q: What did Vikas give Harsha, and why did it help?
qa.a: He gave her a soft rubber ball to squeeze, a safe outlet for her anger along with words for her feeling.

qa.q: How might the neighbour flying the other kite see it?
qa.a: The neighbour might see the cut as part of the kite game, not knowing how upset Harsha felt.

grounding: A child clenches her fists in anger after her kite is cut, and her father offers words and a safe outlet.

passage:
“Ammi! Zaid broke my crayon!”
Farida looked up. Rafiq's fists were balled so tight his knuckles were white.
“Your hands are really squeezing. Are you angry?”
“Very angry!”
“That's a big feeling. Want to squeeze the stress ball or squash the playdough?”
“…Playdough.”
He grabbed the lump and squashed it flat. Then again.
“Better?”
“A little.” He opened his hands. “Can I have the tape to fix it?”
“Let's do it together.”

qa.q: What did Rafiq squash?
qa.a: The playdough.

qa.q: What do Rafiq's white knuckles suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: They show he was very angry that Zaid broke his crayon. The tight squeeze may also have been his way of holding back from hitting.

qa.q: What small step did Farida offer?
qa.a: She named the feeling and gave two safe choices, the stress ball or the playdough, to let the anger out.

qa.q: How might Zaid feel seeing Rafiq's fists?
qa.a: Zaid might feel scared of being hit, and relieved when Farida steered the anger into playdough.

grounding: A preschooler clenches his fists in anger, and his mother offers words for the feeling and a safe outlet.

passage:
Note by Raghav, playgroup leader, Friday.
We played musical chairs. When Eshaan was out, he stood by the wall with his fists clenched and his arms stiff. He didn't cry, but his face was red. I went over and said, “You wanted to win and you're cross.” He nodded hard. I gave him the squishy ball from our calm basket. He squeezed it until the game ended, then asked to help with the music. Next time I'll let the children who are out choose the song.

qa.q: What did Raghav give Eshaan from the calm basket?
qa.a: The squishy ball.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling as he stood by the wall with stiff arms?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated at being out of the game, and his red face suggests he may also have felt embarrassed.

qa.q: What does Raghav plan to change next time, and why?
qa.a: Raghav will let the children who are out choose the song, which gives them a job so being out feels less bad.

qa.q: How might the other children see Eshaan by the wall?
qa.a: They might not notice his clenched fists at all, since he didn't cry or shout.

grounding: The note shows a preschooler clenching his fists in anger and an adult giving words for the feeling and a safe outlet.

passage: At story time in the library in Auckland, Noa sat cross-legged, drumming her fingers on the carpet, then on her knees, then on her shoes. Chen, the librarian, nearly asked her to sit still. Then she noticed that every time she asked a question, Noa's hand shot up first, and she knew the name of every animal in the book. When the story ended, Noa stopped drumming and said, “Again?” Chen smiled and let the drumming be.

qa.q: Where was Noa drumming her fingers?
qa.a: On the carpet, then on her knees, then on her shoes.

qa.q: What does Noa's drumming suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It seems it helped her stay focused and full of interest, since she answered every question first. At first it could have looked like boredom or restlessness.

qa.q: What did Chen do that prevented an unfair scolding?
qa.a: She watched the context, saw that Noa was listening closely, and let the drumming be.

qa.q: How might other adults at story time see Noa's fidgeting?
qa.a: They might think she is bored or not paying attention, unless they notice her answers.

grounding: A child's finger drumming at story time looks like boredom but helps her focus, and the adult watches for context.

passage: The waiting room at the eye clinic was full, and their token was number forty. Sumit drummed his fingers on the plastic chair, swung his legs, and drummed again. A man nearby frowned. Sangeeta, his mother, didn't scold. She saw he'd sat still for an hour. “Bored?” He nodded. “Let's play finger-tap copy.” She tapped a rhythm on her knee; he copied it. Then he made one for her. The drumming turned into a game, and the man began to smile.

qa.q: What number was their token?
qa.a: Number forty.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling while he drummed and swung his legs?
qa.a: He was bored and full of energy after sitting still for an hour. He may also have felt a bit restless in the crowded room.

qa.q: Which choice by Sangeeta worked, and why?
qa.a: She turned the drumming into a copying game, which used his energy and eased his boredom without a scolding.

qa.q: How might the man nearby have seen the drumming at first?
qa.a: He probably found it annoying, but when it became a game he started to smile.

grounding: A child drums his fingers from boredom and energy in a clinic waiting room, and his mother reads the context instead of scolding.

passage: I'm Madhav, Payal's cousin. At our family puja yesterday, the prayers went on for a long time. Payal sat next to me and kept drumming her fingers on her knee. Our aunt leaned over, about to scold her. I noticed Payal was drumming in time with the bell and mouthing the words. I whispered to Aunty, “She's following along.” Aunty watched, then nodded. I don't know for sure if Payal was bored or keeping the beat, but she stayed sitting till the end.

qa.q: What did Payal keep drumming her fingers on?
qa.a: Her knee.

qa.q: What might Payal have been feeling during the long prayers?
qa.a: She might have been interested and focused, since she drummed in time with the bell and mouthed the words. She could also have been a little bored and restless from sitting so long.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that prevented an unfair scolding?
qa.a: Madhav noticed the drumming matched the bell and told the aunt, so she looked again before scolding.

qa.q: How might the aunt have seen the drumming at first?
qa.a: She probably saw it as fidgeting and disrespect during the puja, until Madhav pointed out the beat.

grounding: A cousin observes a child drumming her fingers in a long puja and helps an adult see it may be focus rather than boredom.

passage:
Note by Vidya, KG teacher. Sports day lucky draw.
While we pulled names for the class prize, Preeti sat with both hands crossed, fingers twisted round each other, eyes squeezed shut. When her name wasn't called, she uncrossed them, looked at her fingers and said, “They didn't work.” Her friend showed her their group's secret sign: two taps on the nose, meaning “next time.” Preeti tapped her nose back and grinned. I noticed each little group has its own signs, and they love sharing them. 😊

qa.q: What was the secret sign Preeti's friend showed her?
qa.a: Two taps on the nose, meaning “next time.”

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she said, “They didn't work”?
qa.a: She felt disappointed that her crossed fingers didn't bring luck. She may also have felt a bit puzzled, since she believed in them.

qa.q: How could Vidya use what the note describes about the class's secret signs?
qa.a: Vidya could let the groups teach their signs to each other in a circle time, so the fun is shared and nobody feels left out.

qa.q: How might Preeti's friend see the nose-tap?
qa.a: The friend saw it as a kind way to cheer Preeti up and include her in their shared sign.

grounding: The note shows a preschooler crossing her fingers for luck and enjoying a group's playful secret sign.

passage: At the village school playground, Sunaina hooked her little finger round Disha's. “Pinky promise you'll save me a swing.” Disha looked puzzled and crossed two fingers instead. “In our lane we do this.” “Crossed fingers are for luck!” said Sunaina. “Not in my lane,” Disha giggled. “Crossed means promise.” They tried each other's signs, laughing. In the end they did both, pinkies hooked and fingers crossed, and ran to the swings, which Disha had saved.

qa.q: What does crossed fingers mean in Disha's lane?
qa.a: Promise.

qa.q: What were the girls feeling as they tried each other's signs?
qa.a: They felt amused and playful, enjoying the mix-up. At first Sunaina was a little puzzled that Disha used a different sign.

qa.q: What does this scene show about how to handle different signs?
qa.a: Trying each other's signs and laughing about it works better than insisting only one meaning is right.

qa.q: How might a child from a third lane see their double promise?
qa.a: They might find it confusing or funny, and have their own sign to add, since these signs vary by group.

grounding: Two children find that crossed fingers and pinky promises mean different things in different groups, and enjoy sharing them.

passage: In the kindergarten yard in Melbourne, Bao ran up to Noa and tapped his ear twice. Noa tapped her ear back. That was their secret sign: meet at the sandpit. Before the egg-and-spoon race, Noa crossed her fingers tight behind her back. “For luck,” she whispered. Bao crossed his too, though he wasn't racing. When Noa's egg stayed on the spoon all the way, they both waved crossed fingers in the air and ran to the sandpit together.

qa.q: What did two taps on the ear mean for Bao and Noa?
qa.a: Meet at the sandpit.

qa.q: Why did Bao cross his fingers even though he wasn't racing?
qa.a: He wanted Noa to do well and felt excited and loyal to his friend, sharing her hope for luck.

qa.q: What would you advise a teacher who notices this secret sign?
qa.a: Enjoy it and leave it as their playful thing, while making sure other children are not left out of games.

qa.q: What would change if another child didn't know the ear-tap sign?
qa.a: That child might feel left out or confused, because such signs only work for those who share them.

grounding: Two preschoolers use crossed fingers for luck and a shared secret sign for play.

passage: Daniel's grandmother had flown to London from Pune. At the door, his mother folded her hands and said, “Namaste, Aai.” Daniel copied, pressing his palms together. Grandma's face lit up. Then his friend Elif, visiting from next door, put her right hand over her heart and bowed her head a little, the way her family greeted older people. Grandma laughed and did it back to her. Later, Daniel greeted his grandpa on a video call with both: hands together, then hand on heart.

qa.q: Where had Daniel's grandmother flown from?
qa.a: From Pune.

qa.q: What was Grandma feeling when Daniel pressed his palms together?
qa.a: She was delighted and touched that he greeted her in the way she knew. She may also have felt a bit emotional after a long journey to see him.

qa.q: What helped Daniel learn the greeting?
qa.a: He saw his mother model it warmly at the door and copied her, with no one forcing him.

qa.q: How might Elif's greeting look to Daniel's grandmother?
qa.a: She saw it as a respectful, kind gesture from another family's tradition, and happily returned it.

grounding: A preschooler learns to greet an elder with namaste by copying his mother, and a friend greets with a hand over her heart.

passage: The preschool visited the old people's home near the market. Jagdish Sir walked in first and greeted every resident with folded hands, smiling. Imran watched, then folded his hands too and said a shy “Namaste” to a lady in a shawl. She put her hand on her heart and blessed him. One girl hid behind the door. Jagdish Sir didn't push her. “You can wave, or just watch today,” he said. She waved from the doorway, and a grandpa waved back.

qa.q: What did the lady in a shawl do when Imran greeted her?
qa.a: She put her hand on her heart and blessed him.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he said a shy “Namaste”?
qa.a: He felt shy but wanted to join in, having watched Jagdish Sir greet everyone. After the blessing he likely felt proud.

qa.q: What was wise about how Jagdish Sir handled the girl who hid?
qa.a: He didn't force a greeting and offered a wave or watching, so respect stayed warm rather than pressured.

qa.q: What was it like for the residents to be greeted by the children?
qa.a: They likely felt happy and valued, which showed in the lady's blessing and the grandpa's wave.

grounding: A preschooler learns to greet elders with namaste through warm modelling, and a shy child is not forced.

passage: I'm Kiran, from the house across the lane. Last Sunday Chaitanya's great-grandmother came to stay. When his mother brought him out, Chaitanya hid his face in her sari. His mother didn't pull him. She just folded her hands and greeted the old lady herself. A little later I saw Chaitanya peek out, put his small hand on his chest, and bow his head. The old lady laughed and touched his head. I don't know who taught him that, but he looked pleased.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya hide his face?
qa.a: In his mother's sari.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been feeling when he hid his face?
qa.a: He was probably shy with an elder he did not know well. Later, when he put his hand on his chest, he seemed pleased and more comfortable.

qa.q: Which choice by Chaitanya's mother worked, and why?
qa.a: She didn't pull him out; she greeted the elder herself, which modelled respect and let him choose his own moment.

qa.q: How might the great-grandmother see the little bow?
qa.a: She would likely feel touched and loved, as shown by her laugh and blessing. 🙂

grounding: A neighbour observes a preschooler greet an elder with a hand on his chest after his mother models respect without force.

passage:
“Papa, look at my—”
Amandeep turned from the cot and put a finger to his lips.
Avni froze. Her smile dropped. “Am I in trouble?”
Amandeep came over and knelt, whispering. “No, puttar. Look at my face. Am I cross?”
Avni studied him. His eyes were soft; he was smiling. “No.”
“The baby just fell asleep. My finger means quiet, please, for the baby.”
“Oh.” Avni whispered back, “Look at my drawing, quiet.”
He looked. “Beautiful,” he whispered. 😊

qa.q: Why did Amandeep put a finger to his lips?
qa.a: Because the baby just fell asleep.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she asked, “Am I in trouble?”
qa.a: She felt worried that the finger to the lips meant she had done something wrong. Once she saw his soft eyes and smile, she felt relieved.

qa.q: What small step helped Avni read the gesture correctly?
qa.a: Amandeep asked her to look at his face, so she could see he wasn't cross and learn the setting decides the meaning.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel when Avni thinks she is in trouble?
qa.a: He probably feels a bit sorry that his quick gesture worried her and wants her to know she is welcome.

grounding: A preschooler reads a finger to the lips as trouble and learns, by checking her father's face, that it means quiet for the sleeping baby.

passage:
Library corner note, from Anand, nursery teacher.
Today I put my finger to my lips when the class got loud. Kishore stopped mid-sentence and went pale, staring at me. I realised he thought he was in trouble. I smiled and whispered, “Library voices,” and he smiled back. Some children read the gesture as “You're naughty,” so I will now pair it with a smile. At home, you may like to show Kishore how a finger on the lips can mean different things: quiet, a surprise, or a sleeping baby.

qa.q: What did Anand whisper to Kishore?
qa.a: “Library voices.”

qa.q: What does Kishore going pale suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt scared that he was in trouble. He may also have felt embarrassed being looked at in front of the class.

qa.q: What change does Anand plan, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Anand will pair the gesture with a smile, so children can read from the teacher's face that it means quiet, not that they are in trouble.

qa.q: How might Kishore's parents use the note?
qa.a: They could help Kishore learn the different meanings of a finger to the lips by showing him examples at home.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler misreading a finger to the lips as trouble until the teacher's face shows it only means quiet.

passage: In the village hide-and-seek game, Vijay squeezed into the haystack beside Samir. As footsteps came near, Vijay put a finger to his lips, eyes sparkling. Samir clapped a hand over his mouth to hold in a giggle. The seeker walked past. Later, back home, Samir's grandmother did the same finger-to-lips when he ran in shouting, and he stopped short. Then he saw her pointing at Dada, asleep on the charpai. Samir tiptoed past, finger on his own lips.

qa.q: Where did Vijay and Samir hide?
qa.a: In the haystack.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he clapped a hand over his mouth?
qa.a: He was excited and giggly, trying hard not to be found. He trusted Vijay's sparkling eyes that the gesture was part of the game.

qa.q: How did Samir work out what his grandmother's gesture meant?
qa.a: He looked at the setting, saw her pointing at Dada asleep, and understood it meant be quiet for Dada.

qa.q: What would change if Samir hadn't looked at where his grandmother was pointing?
qa.a: He might have thought he was in trouble for shouting, instead of knowing he only needed to be quiet.

grounding: A preschooler reads a finger to the lips differently in a game and at home, using the setting to decide its meaning.

passage: In the KG classroom, Reena Ma'am was reading about a lost puppy. Pallavi's hand shot up and stayed there. She bounced on her knees, then held her arm up with her other hand. Reena noticed and gave her a quick nod. “One minute, Pallavi, I see you.” Pallavi pressed her knees together and bounced faster. At the end of the page, Reena called on her. “Can I go to the toilet?” Reena smiled. “Of course. Next time you can show me the toilet sign, and go.”

qa.q: What was Reena Ma'am reading about?
qa.a: A lost puppy.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling as she bounced and held her arm up?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable and anxious because she needed the toilet, and it was hard to wait. Her teacher could not tell at first whether it was a question or excitement.

qa.q: What small step did Reena offer so waiting would be easier next time?
qa.a: She suggested a toilet sign, so Pallavi could signal what she needed and go without waiting for her turn to speak.

qa.q: What is it like for Reena to see a hand that stays up for a long time?
qa.a: She has to guess whether it is eagerness, a question or a need, so a quick nod helps the child while she finishes the page.

grounding: A child raises her hand and struggles to wait, the gesture turning out to mean a toilet need, and the teacher's quick nod eases the wait.

passage: I'm Bidisha, a parent helper on reading day. Aadhya sat right in front. Every time the teacher asked a question, she shouted the answer. The teacher reminded her, “Hands up, please.” The next time Aadhya's hand went up so fast she nearly fell over, and she kept saying “Me! Me!” under her breath. The teacher caught her eye and nodded, then called another child first. Aadhya's face crumpled, but she kept her hand up. Next question, the teacher picked her, and her whole face lit up.

qa.q: What did the teacher remind Aadhya to do?
qa.a: Put her hand up.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when her face crumpled?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and disappointed that another child was picked while she was trying so hard to wait. Bidisha could only see her face, so she might also have felt unsure if she would ever get a turn.

qa.q: How did the teacher's nod help Aadhya?
qa.a: It showed Aadhya that her raised hand was seen, which helped her keep waiting instead of blurting out.

qa.q: How might the other children see Aadhya's shouting before she raised her hand?
qa.a: They might feel it was unfair that she answered first each time, which is why hands up gives everyone a turn.

grounding: A parent helper observes a child learning to raise her hand instead of blurting, with the teacher's quick nod easing her frustration.

passage:
Week one: Suraj called out every answer before Farida Miss finished the question. Other children stopped trying.
Week two: Farida Miss taught hands up. Suraj raised his, but waiting was so hard he groaned and slapped the desk. Farida Miss gave him a quick nod each time. “I see you, Suraj. You're next.”
Week three: Suraj raised his hand and waited, lips pressed together, eyes on Farida Miss. When she nodded, he grinned and sat on his hands. When she called him, he said, “Can I say two answers?”

qa.q: What did Suraj do in week one?
qa.a: He called out every answer before Farida Miss finished the question.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling in week two when he groaned and slapped the desk?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, because he was eager to answer and waiting was hard. The raised hand showed his excitement.

qa.q: Which step helped Suraj most, and why?
qa.a: Farida Miss's quick nod and “You're next” showed him he had been seen, which made waiting easier.

qa.q: How might the other children feel by week three?
qa.a: They would likely feel more willing to answer, since Suraj was no longer calling out first every time.

grounding: Over three weeks, a child learns to raise his hand and wait, with the teacher's nod easing his frustration.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Chinmay held his arm and wouldn't talk. Nurse Indu knelt. “Can you show me what happened?” Chinmay stood up, pretended to hold two chains, swung his legs forward, then let go of the chains and flopped onto his side. “You fell off a swing?” He nodded. “And where does it hurt?” He mimed hitting the ground with his elbow, then pointed at it. “Thank you,” said Indu. “That was very clear.” Chinmay sat down, a little less pale.

qa.q: How did Chinmay show he fell?
qa.a: He pretended to hold two chains, swung his legs forward, then let go and flopped onto his side.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have mimed instead of talking?
qa.a: He was probably shy with the nurse and scared about his sore arm, so miming felt easier than finding words.

qa.q: What did Indu do that helped Chinmay explain?
qa.a: She asked him to show her, guessed out loud, and thanked him, so he could explain without words.

qa.q: How might Indu feel when the mime makes things clear?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved to know how he got hurt, which helps her decide what to check.

grounding: A shy preschooler at a clinic uses mime to explain how he got hurt when words fail.

passage: I'm Kavitha, Aditi's big sister. Today Aditi set her dolls in a row and poured them tea from an empty hand, lifting her little finger like Nani does. Then she pretended to drive them to the market, turning a steering wheel that wasn't there and going “Pom pom!” Later she ran to Nani, flapping her arms and pointing at the window. Nani said, “A crow?” Aditi shook her head and flapped harder. Nani tried, “A big bird?” Aditi shouted, “Peacock!” We all ran to see it.

qa.q: What did Aditi pretend to drive?
qa.a: She pretended to drive her dolls to the market, turning a steering wheel that wasn't there.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she flapped harder after Nani guessed a crow?
qa.a: She was excited and a bit frustrated that Nani didn't guess right, and wanted everyone to see what she saw.

qa.q: What could Nani do when a child's mime is hard to guess?
qa.a: She could keep guessing and ask simple questions, as she did, until Aditi found the word.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Aditi's miming?
qa.a: Kavitha sees it as playful and imaginative, and enjoys how it helped everyone find the peacock.

grounding: An older sister observes a preschooler miming tea, driving and a bird to play and to explain what she saw.

passage:
Monday: Aditi was new in the class and hadn't said a word. At snack time she lifted an empty hand to her mouth and tipped it. Karthik Sir guessed, “Water?” She nodded, and he filled her cup.
Wednesday: She mimed a bird flying and pointed at the window. Sir guessed, “You want to see the birds?” She nodded again, but looked disappointed when he didn't take her outside.
Friday: She mimed drinking and whispered, “Water.” Sir smiled wide. “Here you go, Aditi.”

qa.q: What did Aditi mime at snack time on Monday?
qa.a: She lifted an empty hand to her mouth and tipped it.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling on Wednesday when Sir didn't take her outside?
qa.a: She felt disappointed, because she wanted him to understand her mime and act on it. Being shy, she was still expecting adults to guess her meaning.

qa.q: What could Karthik Sir try next to help Aditi use words?
qa.a: He could guess, then say the word slowly and wait a moment, giving Aditi space to repeat it.

qa.q: How might Karthik Sir feel when Aditi whispers “Water” on Friday?
qa.a: He is probably pleased and proud of her, which shows in his wide smile. 😊

grounding: Over a week, a shy new preschooler uses mime to communicate, then begins to add words.

passage: I'm Rekha, from the house by the pond. This morning I saw Yamini come running back from fishing with her grandfather. “Aunty! I caught a fish this big!” She stretched her arms out as wide as they would go, then wider, nearly falling over. Her grandfather held up a small fish, about the size of his palm, and winked at me. Yamini didn't notice. She was jumping. I said, “That's a very big catch!” I don't know if she thought it was really that size, but she was bursting with pride.

qa.q: What did Yamini's grandfather hold up?
qa.a: A small fish, about the size of his palm.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she stretched her arms wider and wider?
qa.a: She was excited and proud of her catch, and the wide arms showed how big it felt to her rather than its real size.

qa.q: What was wise about Rekha's reply?
qa.a: Rekha shared Yamini's joy instead of correcting the size, since the gesture was about excitement, not accuracy.

qa.q: How might the grandfather see the arm-spreading?
qa.a: He finds it sweet and funny, which is why he winked at Rekha while holding up the small fish.

grounding: A neighbour observes a child spreading her arms to show a fish's size, exaggerating from excitement rather than accuracy.

passage:
A month before: “How old will you be?” Madhav asked his little sister. Gurpreet held up four fingers, then five, then three, giggling.
A week before: Gurpreet practised with her hand in her lap, folding down her thumb and opening it. “Five!”
Birthday: The guests asked, “How old are you?” Gurpreet held up five fingers proudly. Then she spread her arms wide. “And my cake is THIS big!” Madhav laughed; the cake was only the size of a plate, but it was her favourite.

qa.q: How big was the cake really?
qa.a: Only the size of a plate.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling on her birthday when she spread her arms wide?
qa.a: She was excited and proud, using her arms to show how big her joy felt, not the cake's actual size.

qa.q: What helped Gurpreet show her age correctly?
qa.a: She practised in the weeks before, folding and opening her thumb until five fingers came out right.

qa.q: How does Madhav see Gurpreet's “THIS big” cake?
qa.a: He finds it funny and sweet, knowing the cake is small but that she is excited.

grounding: A preschooler learns to show her age on her fingers over a month and spreads her arms to show excitement about her cake.

passage: The market was loud with sellers shouting, and Shreya had only twenty rupees left. “Ojas, how many balloons?” she asked. He couldn't hear. He held up three fingers, then spread his arms very wide. Shreya bent down. “Three big ones? I only have money for one.” Ojas held up one finger, then slowly brought his arms in to a small circle. “One small one?” He nodded hard. She bought a small red balloon, and Ojas held it like a treasure all the way to the bus.

qa.q: How much money did Shreya have left?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he spread his arms very wide?
qa.a: He was excited about the balloons and wanted big ones. Later, bringing his arms in to a small circle showed he accepted one small balloon without getting upset.

qa.q: What did Shreya do well in the noisy market?
qa.a: She bent down, read his finger and arm signs, and said aloud what she understood so they could agree.

qa.q: What would change if the market were quiet?
qa.a: Ojas could have just said what he wanted, but he might still have used his arms to show his excitement.

grounding: A child uses fingers and arm spreads to show number and size in a noisy market, with some excitement-driven exaggeration.

passage:
Monday: Ayesha came home from school, didn't take off her shoes, and curled up in the corner of the sofa, knees to chin. Sudha Nani didn't ask questions. She sat at the other end, knitting.
Tuesday: The same. Nani brought her warm milk and sat nearby, quietly.
Wednesday: Ayesha shuffled over and leaned on Nani. “They laughed at my plaits.” Nani stopped knitting. “That's not kind. Thank you for telling me.” That evening, Nani phoned the class teacher, who promised to speak to the children the next morning.

qa.q: What did Nani bring Ayesha on Tuesday?
qa.a: Warm milk.

qa.q: What does Ayesha curling up with her knees to her chin suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt sad and ashamed, and wanted to hide after being teased. Nani could not be sure at first what had happened.

qa.q: What did Nani do when Ayesha finally told her?
qa.a: She thanked her for telling, said the teasing was not kind, and phoned the class teacher that same evening.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see Nani's phone call?
qa.a: The teacher would likely be glad to know, so the children who laughed can be spoken to the next morning.

grounding: Over three days, a child curls up after being teased, and her grandmother's quiet presence helps her open up.

passage: The house was full of guests for Diwali, and Chandrika had three pans on the stove. She'd snapped at Siddharth for knocking over the rangoli colours. Now he was nowhere. She found him behind the curtain, hunched on the floor, chin tucked, arms wrapped round his knees. Guests were calling her. Chandrika sat down beside him anyway, saying nothing. After a minute, he leaned his head on her arm. “I'm sorry I shouted,” she said softly. He nodded, and she held him a moment longer.

qa.q: Where did Chandrika find Siddharth?
qa.a: Behind the curtain, hunched on the floor.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been feeling when he hunched behind the curtain?
qa.a: He likely felt ashamed and sad after being snapped at for spilling the rangoli colours, and wanted to hide. He may also have felt overwhelmed by the busy house.

qa.q: What worked for Chandrika even with little time?
qa.a: She sat quietly beside him instead of asking many questions, and apologised gently once he leaned on her.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to leave the guests and pans?
qa.a: It is hard, since everyone needs her, but she chose to give Siddharth her quiet presence first.

grounding: A child curls inward after being scolded during a busy festival, and his mother's quiet presence helps.

passage: Wasim came in from the colony park, went straight to the sofa and curled up, his face pressed into a cushion. His glasses lay on the floor. Jahnavi Phuppo put down her book. She didn't ask “What happened?” She just sat at the end of the sofa and gently rubbed his foot. After a while he mumbled into the cushion, “They called me four-eyes.” Phuppo said, “That was unkind, and it's not true about you.” She told his parents that evening, and they went to talk to the other boys' parents.

qa.q: What lay on the floor?
qa.a: Wasim's glasses.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he curled up with his face in the cushion?
qa.a: He was hurt and sad about being called names, and probably wanted to hide. He may also have felt embarrassed about his glasses.

qa.q: What made it easier for Wasim to speak?
qa.a: Phuppo stayed calm and close without questioning, so he felt safe enough to tell her.

qa.q: How might Wasim's parents feel when Phuppo tells them?
qa.a: They would likely feel upset for him and protective, which is why they went to talk to the other boys' parents.

grounding: A child curls inward after being teased, and his aunt's quiet presence helps him share it.
